questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Given a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],
$$

the inverse of $B$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(B)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(B)=2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1=-1
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(B)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B{B}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {B}^{-1}B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Given a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
E=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],
$$

the inverse of $E$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(E)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(E)=4\cdot 7-8\cdot 3=4
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(E)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}E{E}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {E}^{-1}E & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the matrices below does **not** have an inverse?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 5 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
- The matrix $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix. So, it is not invertible.

- For the matrix $B$, we have

$$
det(B)=6\cdot 4-8\cdot 3=0.
$$

Because $det(B)=0,$ we conclude that $B$ is not invertible.

- For the matrix $C$, we have

$$
det(C)=(-1)\cdot 5-1\cdot 5=-10.
$$

Because $det(C)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $C$ is invertible.

Therefore, only $A$ and $B$ do not have an inverse.

questions.problem:
Which of the matrices below are singular?

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 & 7 & -6 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -4\end{aligned}],\,U=[\begin{aligned}3 & -15 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
- The matrix $T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix. So, it is not invertible. Since the matrix is not square, we can't say that it's singular.

- For the matrix $U$, we have

$$
det(U)=3\cdot 4-(-1)\cdot (-15)=-3.
$$

Because $det(U)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $U$ is invertible.

- For the matrix $V$, we have

$$
det(V)=6\cdot 5-10\cdot 3=0.
$$

Because $det(V)=0,$ we conclude that $V$ is not invertible. Since $V$ is a square matrix that is not invertible, we also say that $V$ is singular.

Therefore, only $V$ is singular.

questions.problem: If $H=[\begin{aligned}5 & c \\ c & 5\end{aligned}]$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $c.$
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $H$ is singular if and only if $det(H)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(H) & =5\cdot 5-c\cdot c \\  & =25-{c}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}25-{c}^{2} & =0 \\ {c}^{2} & =25 \\ c & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the values of $c$ are $c=\pm 5.$

$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a $2 \times 2$ matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

the inverse of $A$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
\det(A) = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot (-2) = 1
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}]. \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -0 \\ -(-2) & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {A}^{-1}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving for a Variable in a Singular Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
If 
$[\begin{aligned}1-k & 2 \\ 2 & 1-k\end{aligned}]$
 is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $k.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ is singular if and only if $\det(A)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(1-k)(1-k)-4 \\  & ={k}^{2}-2k-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{k}^{2}-2k-3 & =0 \\ (k-3)(k+1) & =0 \\ k & =3,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the values of $k$ are $k=3$ and $k=-1.$
